summary: Nora's after-the-turn review now counts putting one person's words in another person's mouth as an unsupported claim. Until now it only asked whether somebody in the room had said the thing, never who.
details: The review reads a finished exchange and says whether everything Nora asserted was backed by what she actually had. Quoting a real line under the wrong name passed that check: the words were said, by someone, and the review was told in as many words that it was judging sourcing rather than correctness. Naming a speaker is a claim about who, so it is now judged the same way as any other claim.
When the review does flag one, it says whose words were given to whom, so the entry is readable without re-reading the conversation.
This matters beyond the score. A turn the review passes feeds the running position Nora carries into the next turn, so a wrong name used to survive and be treated as settled from then on.
Nothing new is collected to make this work: the conversation the review reads has always named the speaker on every line.
limitations: The review is a judgement, not a check that can be proved right — it can still miss one, and it can flag a quote Nora attributed correctly. What changed is that a misattribution is now the kind of thing it is looking for.
